concepts.def: The mechanism driving evolutionary change: individuals in a population vary in heritable traits, more offspring are produced than can survive, and those whose traits are better adapted to the selection pressures of their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the alleles they carry become more frequent in the population over generations. It has operated continuously over billions of years and is the source of the biodiversity of life on Earth.

A fundamental change in the accepted framework of ideas within which scientists interpret observations. In Darwin's time it was widely accepted that species evolved, but the mechanism was unclear; Darwin's theory of natural selection supplied a convincing mechanism and replaced Lamarckism, which is an example of a paradigm shift.

The earlier explanation of evolutionary change, associated with Lamarck, in which characteristics acquired by an individual during its lifetime through use, disuse or the environment are passed on to its offspring. It was replaced by Darwin's mechanism of natural selection because acquired characteristics are not encoded in genes and so are not heritable.

concepts.term: Mutation as a source of variation
concepts.def: A change in the base sequence of DNA. Mutation is the only source of new alleles: it generates the new heritable variants on which natural selection can act, and it occurs randomly rather than in response to the needs of the organism.

concepts.term: Sexual reproduction as a source of variation
concepts.def: Meiosis (through crossing over and the random orientation of bivalents) and the random fusion of gametes at fertilization produce offspring with new combinations of existing alleles. Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles; it generates new combinations of the alleles already present.

The tendency of populations to produce more offspring than the environment can support. Because more individuals are produced than can survive to reproduce, individuals compete for limited resources, and this competition is a factor that promotes natural selection.

The maximum population size of a species that a particular environment can sustain over time, set by the limiting resources available. Food is one such resource; others include water, light, space, nesting or breeding sites, and shelter from predators and weather.

A non-living component of the environment, such as temperature, water availability, light intensity, salinity or soil pH, that can affect the survival of individuals and so act as a selection pressure on a population.

A factor whose effect on the proportion of individuals surviving does not depend on the density (number per unit area) of the population. Abiotic factors such as unusually high or low temperatures, drought, flooding or fire are typically density-independent: they can kill a similar proportion of a crowded population and a sparse one.

Any factor in the environment, biotic or abiotic, that affects the chances of survival and reproduction of individuals with particular heritable traits, and so changes which alleles are passed on to the next generation.

A heritable characteristic that makes an individual better suited to its environment and so increases its chances of survival and reproduction. Individuals within a population differ in how well adapted they are, and these differences are the basis of natural selection.

The survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype: how successful individuals with that genotype are at surviving and leaving offspring that themselves survive, relative to other genotypes in the population. Fitness is not physical strength or size; a genotype that produces more surviving offspring has higher fitness.

Competition between individuals of the same species for the same limited resources or for mates. Because these individuals differ in their adaptations, some survive and reproduce more successfully than others, and this is the competition on which natural selection is based.

A characteristic that is determined by an individual's genes, encoded in the base sequence of its DNA, and so can be passed on to offspring through the gametes. Only heritable traits can be changed in frequency by natural selection, so traits must be heritable for evolutionary change to occur.

A characteristic that develops during an individual's life as a result of environmental factors, such as enlarged muscles from exercise, scars, or skills that have been learned. Acquired characteristics are not encoded in the base sequence of genes and so are not heritable.

A selection pressure in animal species arising from differences in success at attracting or competing for a mate. Physical and behavioural traits that can be used as signs of overall fitness, such as plumage, size or courtship display, increase mating success, so the alleles for them become more frequent even when they carry a survival cost.

The elaborate, brightly coloured feathers and courtship displays of male birds of paradise, used as an example of sexual selection: females choose males with the most impressive plumage and display, so alleles for these traits have increased in frequency over generations even though the plumage is costly to grow and makes males more conspicuous.

John Endler's experiments with guppies (Poecilia reticulata) from streams in Trinidad, in which he controlled the selection pressures experimentally. In artificial ponds and in stream transplants he varied the presence of predators (the dangerous pike cichlid Crenicichla and the weaker predator Rivulus) and the size of the gravel. Where predation was strong, males evolved fewer, smaller and duller spots; where predators were absent, sexual selection by females produced more numerous, larger and brighter spots within a few generations.
All the genes, and their different alleles, present in a population. Natural selection, mutation, migration and genetic drift change the frequencies of alleles in the gene pool over generations.

The proportion of all the copies of a gene in a population's gene pool that are a particular allele, expressed as a decimal fraction between 0 and 1 or as a percentage. In a diploid population each individual contributes two copies of each autosomal gene, so allele frequency is not the same as the proportion of individuals showing a phenotype or carrying the allele.

Populations of the same species that are separated by a physical barrier so that little or no interbreeding occurs between them. Because their gene pools are separate, natural selection, genetic drift and founder effects can lead them to have different allele frequencies. Allele-frequency databases show this for human populations: for example, the frequencies of the ABO blood group alleles differ markedly between populations in different parts of the world.

The integration of genetics with Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection. It explains evolution as a change in allele frequencies in the gene pool, with mutation generating new alleles and natural selection acting on individuals according to differences in their heritable traits, so that alleles conferring higher fitness increase in frequency.

Selection that favours individuals at one extreme of the range of variation in a trait, so that the mean of the trait shifts in that direction over generations and the frequency of the alleles for that extreme increases. An example is the increase in antibiotic resistance in bacteria exposed to an antibiotic.

Selection that favours individuals at both extremes of the range of variation over those with intermediate values, so that the population becomes more variable or divides into two distinct forms, and allele frequencies change in favour of the alleles for the extremes.

Selection that favours individuals with intermediate values of a trait over those at either extreme, so that the mean stays the same but variation is reduced. Allele frequencies still change, because the alleles for the extreme phenotypes are removed from the gene pool.

For a gene with two alleles whose frequencies are p and q, p + q = 1, and if the population is in genetic equilibrium the genotype frequencies are given by p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p² is the frequency of one homozygote, q² the frequency of the other homozygote and 2pq the frequency of heterozygotes. If one genotype frequency is known (usually the homozygous recessive, q²), the allele frequencies can be calculated from it.

The state of a population in which allele frequencies, and hence genotype frequencies, remain constant from generation to generation, so that the genotype frequencies fit the Hardy–Weinberg equation. A population in genetic equilibrium is not evolving.

The conditions that must be maintained for a population to remain in genetic equilibrium: the population is large, mating is random, there is no mutation, no migration into or out of the population, and no natural selection (all genotypes have equal survival and reproductive success). If observed genotype frequencies do not fit the Hardy–Weinberg equation, one or more of these conditions is not being met.

Selection by deliberate human choice of traits: in crop plants and domesticated animals, humans choose the individuals with desirable traits to breed from, so the alleles for those traits increase in frequency over generations. Unintended consequences of human actions, such as the evolution of antibiotic resistance in bacteria, are due to natural rather than artificial selection.

mcqs.q: The replacement of Lamarckism by Darwin's theory of natural selection is described as a paradigm shift. What does the term 'paradigm shift' mean?
options: A fundamental change in the framework of ideas within which scientists explain their observations
The first proposal by any scientist that species change over time rather than being fixed
The acceptance that characteristics acquired during life are passed on to offspring
A discovery that proves a scientific theory correct beyond any further doubt
mcqs.specStatementText: Natural selection: the mechanism, and the paradigm shift it caused
mcqs.explain: A paradigm is the accepted framework of ideas within which observations are interpreted. Darwin's mechanism replaced Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics as the framework for explaining evolutionary change, so the change is a paradigm shift.
rationales: A paradigm is the accepted framework of ideas within which observations are interpreted. Darwin's mechanism replaced Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics as the framework for explaining evolutionary change, so the change is a paradigm shift.

A student who thinks Darwin discovered evolution itself picks this. In Darwin's time it was already widely understood that species evolved; what was unclear was the mechanism, and it was the mechanism that shifted.

A student who believes acquired characteristics are inherited assumes that this is the accepted modern explanation and so names it as the new framework. It is in fact Lamarckism, the framework that was replaced; acquired characteristics are not encoded in genes and so are not heritable.

A student who thinks science proves theories once and for all picks this. Scientific theories are not proved beyond doubt; Darwin's theory was later extended by genetics into neo-Darwinism, showing the framework can still develop.

mcqs.q: Which statement about natural selection as the mechanism of evolutionary change is correct?
options: It produced the species that exist today and has now stopped acting upon any of them
It has operated continuously over billions of years and is still operating today
It causes the mutations that individuals need to survive new conditions
It acts to improve each species as a whole rather than on individual organisms
mcqs.specStatementText: Natural selection: the mechanism, and the paradigm shift it caused
mcqs.explain: Natural selection operates wherever there is heritable variation, overproduction and a selection pressure. It has acted continuously over billions of years to produce the biodiversity of life on Earth and continues in every population now.
rationales: A student who files natural selection under history picks this. Selection pressures still operate on every population; the evolution of antibiotic resistance is a present-day example.

Natural selection operates wherever there is heritable variation, overproduction and a selection pressure. It has acted continuously over billions of years to produce the biodiversity of life on Earth and continues in every population now.
A student who thinks organisms produce the alleles they need picks this. Mutation is random and precedes selection; natural selection changes the frequencies of alleles that already exist.

A student who takes the species as the unit of selection picks this. Natural selection acts on differences between individuals in survival and reproduction; alleles spread because they raise the fitness of the individuals carrying them.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the roles of mutation and sexual reproduction in generating the variation on which natural selection acts?
options: Sexual reproduction produces new alleles by combining together the DNA of two different parents
Mutation produces precisely the particular alleles that the environment requires for survival
Mutation produces new alleles, and sexual reproduction produces new combinations of alleles
A trait can spread only once a new mutation for it arises, as populations lack variation
mcqs.explain: Mutation is the only source of new alleles. Meiosis and random fertilization then shuffle the alleles that already exist into new combinations in the offspring, so both processes contribute variation but in different ways.
rationales: A student who thinks mixing parental DNA makes new alleles picks this. Every allele in an offspring came from a parent; sexual reproduction creates new combinations, not new alleles.
A student who thinks mutations are directed by need picks this. Mutations are random changes in base sequence and occur whether or not they are useful; selection acts afterwards.

Mutation is the only source of new alleles. Meiosis and random fertilization then shuffle the alleles that already exist into new combinations in the offspring, so both processes contribute variation but in different ways.

A student who underestimates how much heritable variation an ordinary population already contains picks this. Mutation has been generating alleles continuously, so populations already carry the variation on which selection acts.

mcqs.q: A pair of blue tits can raise about ten chicks each year, yet the number of blue tits in a woodland stays roughly constant from year to year. How does this promote natural selection?
options: Overproduction plays no part, because chicks with the better alleles would survive equally well without competition
The chicks compete for food only, because nesting sites, territory and other resources are not limiting in a woodland
The chicks compete mainly with other bird species, and competition between blue tits themselves is unimportant
Far more chicks are produced than the limited resources can support, so they compete and only some survive
mcqs.specStatementText: Too many offspring, too few resources
mcqs.explain: Overproduction of offspring combined with limited food, nesting sites and territories means the woodland is at its carrying capacity. Chicks compete, and those whose heritable traits give them an advantage are more likely to survive and breed.
rationales: A student who reduces natural selection to 'the best adapted survive' picks this. Without overproduction and competition, small differences in adaptation would make little difference to survival.

A student who names food as the only resource picks this. Carrying capacity can be set by any limiting resource, including nesting holes, territory, water and shelter, and blue tits compete for all of these.
A student who sees selection as a contest between species picks this. The strongest competition is intraspecific, because blue tits need exactly the same food, nest sites and mates as each other.

Overproduction of offspring combined with limited food, nesting sites and territories means the woodland is at its carrying capacity. Chicks compete, and those whose heritable traits give them an advantage are more likely to survive and breed.

mcqs.q: An unusually cold winter kills 70% of a population of lizards. The proportion killed is similar in crowded and in sparse populations. Which statement is correct?
options: Low temperature is a density-independent abiotic selection pressure: lizards better able to tolerate cold are likelier to survive and breed
Temperature cannot be a selection pressure, because the deaths were not the result of competition between the lizards
The cold acted as a density-dependent factor, because it killed such a large number of lizards in the population
The surviving lizards became more cold-tolerant during the winter and will pass this tolerance on to their offspring
mcqs.explain: Extreme temperature is an abiotic factor whose effect does not depend on population density. Provided cold tolerance is partly heritable, the survivors are not a random sample, so allele frequencies in the population change.
rationales: Extreme temperature is an abiotic factor whose effect does not depend on population density. Provided cold tolerance is partly heritable, the survivors are not a random sample, so allele frequencies in the population change.
A student who equates selection with contests between organisms picks this. Any factor, biotic or abiotic, that affects survival according to heritable traits is a selection pressure.

A student who reads 'density-dependent' as 'kills a lot' picks this. Density dependence is about whether the proportion affected changes with crowding; here it did not, so the factor is density-independent.

A student who thinks individuals adapt and pass the change on picks this. Tolerance acquired during life is not encoded in the base sequence of genes; the survivors were those that already carried alleles for greater cold tolerance.

mcqs.q: In a population of red deer, stag X is the largest and strongest male but leaves two offspring that survive to breed. Stag Y is smaller and weaker but leaves six offspring that survive to breed. Which stag has the higher fitness, and why?
options: Stag X, because fitness means the physical strength and bodily condition of the individual animal
Stag Y, because fitness is measured by the number of surviving offspring a genotype contributes
Stag X, because natural selection favours traits that aid survival rather than reproduction
Neither, because fitness is a property of the deer species as a whole and not of individuals
mcqs.specStatementText: Adaptation, fitness and competition within a species
mcqs.explain: Fitness is the survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype: its contribution to the next generation. Stag Y's genotype is represented by three times as many offspring, so it has the higher fitness whatever its size.
rationales: A student who uses the everyday meaning of fitness picks this. In natural selection, strength matters only if it leads to more surviving offspring, and here it did not.

Fitness is the survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype: its contribution to the next generation. Stag Y's genotype is represented by three times as many offspring, so it has the higher fitness whatever its size.

A student who thinks selection is only about survival picks this. Fitness depends on both survival and reproduction; an allele that increases offspring number spreads even in a smaller, weaker animal.

A student who takes the species as the unit of selection picks this. Fitness is defined for genotypes and compared between individuals of the same species; that comparison is the basis of natural selection.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the basis of natural selection due to intraspecific competition?
options: Different species compete with one another, and the species that has the best adaptations survives
Individuals improve their adaptations during life, and the improved ones out-compete the rest
Individuals of one species differ in adaptation, so some survive and reproduce more than others
The strongest individuals win fights for resources, and strength is what biologists mean by fitness
mcqs.specStatementText: Adaptation, fitness and competition within a species
mcqs.explain: Members of a species compete for the same resources and mates. Because they differ in heritable adaptations, they differ in survival and reproduction, and this difference is what natural selection acts on.
rationales: A student who treats the species as the unit of competition picks this. Natural selection arises from differences between individuals within a species, which use exactly the same resources.
A student who thinks of adaptation as something an individual does picks this. Adaptations are heritable traits individuals are born with; improvements acquired during life are not inherited.

Members of a species compete for the same resources and mates. Because they differ in heritable adaptations, they differ in survival and reproduction, and this difference is what natural selection acts on.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of fitness picks this. Fitness is the survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype; strength contributes only where it increases surviving offspring.

mcqs.q: A woman develops large, strong arm muscles through years of rowing training. Will her children inherit larger arm muscles as a result of her training?
options: Yes, because characteristics that an individual acquires during life are passed on to its offspring
Yes, if she teaches her children to row, because anything passed from parent to child is heritable
Yes, because the training causes mutations in the genes for muscle growth that her children will receive
No, because muscle growth caused by training is not encoded in the base sequence of her genes
mcqs.explain: Enlarged muscles are an acquired characteristic caused by an environmental factor. Only traits encoded in the base sequence of DNA are passed on through gametes, so her training cannot be inherited; her children inherit only her alleles.
rationales: A student who holds the Lamarckian view picks this. Acquired characteristics are not heritable, which is why Darwin's mechanism replaced Lamarckism.
A student who uses the everyday meaning of 'inherit' picks this. A skill learned from a parent is acquired, not heritable; heritable traits are those determined by genes.
A student who thinks mutations arise in response to need picks this. Mutations are random changes in base sequence, and exercise does not direct mutations into the gametes.

Enlarged muscles are an acquired characteristic caused by an environmental factor. Only traits encoded in the base sequence of DNA are passed on through gametes, so her training cannot be inherited; her children inherit only her alleles.

mcqs.q: Male birds of paradise have elaborate, brightly coloured plumage and perform complex courtship displays, while females are dull. The plumage is costly to grow and makes males easier for predators to see. Which explains how this plumage evolved?
options: Females mate preferentially with males whose plumage signals overall fitness, so alleles for elaborate plumage rise in frequency
The plumage cannot have evolved by selection, because a trait that lowers survival is selected against rather than favoured
The plumage evolved by artificial selection, because each female deliberately chooses which male's traits are passed on
Males that display more often grow brighter plumage during their lives and pass the brighter plumage on to their sons
mcqs.explain: This is sexual selection. Differences in physical and behavioural traits that act as signs of overall fitness affect success in attracting a mate, so males with the most elaborate plumage leave more offspring despite the survival cost.
rationales: This is sexual selection. Differences in physical and behavioural traits that act as signs of overall fitness affect success in attracting a mate, so males with the most elaborate plumage leave more offspring despite the survival cost.
A student who thinks selection is only about survival picks this. Fitness includes reproduction; if the gain in mating success outweighs the survival cost, the alleles for the plumage spread.

A student who equates 'choice' with artificial selection picks this. Artificial selection is deliberate choice of traits by humans; mate choice within a species is a selection pressure arising in the animal's own environment, with no human involved.
A student who thinks acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Plumage developed through use is not encoded in genes; the alleles for elaborate plumage were inherited and selected.

mcqs.q: In elephant seals, males fight for control of a stretch of beach, and the largest males mate with most of the females there. Which statement about the evolution of large body size in male elephant seals is correct?
options: Large males have the higher fitness simply because they are stronger, whether or not they succeed in mating
Large size is favoured by sexual selection because it increases a male's success in competing for mates
Fighting for mates is not a selection pressure, since only survival differences drive evolution
Large size evolved because it benefits the species by ensuring only the best genes are passed on
mcqs.explain: Sexual selection is a selection pressure arising from differences in mating success. Large males win fights, mate with more females and leave more offspring, so alleles for large size have increased in frequency in males.
rationales: A student who uses the everyday meaning of fitness picks this. Fitness is reproductive potential; large size raises fitness here only because it leads to more offspring.

Sexual selection is a selection pressure arising from differences in mating success. Large males win fights, mate with more females and leave more offspring, so alleles for large size have increased in frequency in males.
A student who thinks selection is only about survival picks this. Differences in reproductive success change allele frequencies just as differences in survival do.

A student who thinks selection works for the good of the species picks this. Alleles for large size spread because they raise the fitness of the individual males carrying them, not for any benefit to the species.

mcqs.q: Endler transferred guppies from a stream containing the dangerous predator Crenicichla to a stream that had no guppies and only the weak predator Rivulus, which rarely eats adult guppies. Two years later, the males in the new stream had on average more coloured spots, and larger spots, than the population they came from. Which is the best interpretation?
options: The result shows that predators and females favour the same trait, so the two pressures added together to increase spots
New mutations for extra spots must have arisen during the two years, because the trait could not have spread without them
With strong predation removed, female preference for spotted males was no longer opposed by selection for camouflage
Individual males developed more spots once they were safer from predators and passed the new spots to their sons
mcqs.specStatementText: Endler's guppies: selection pressures under experimental control
mcqs.explain: In the original stream, natural selection by Crenicichla favoured dull, small-spotted males while females favoured bright ones. Moving the fish to a stream with only a weak predator greatly reduced one of the two opposing pressures, so alleles for more and larger spots increased in frequency.
rationales: A student who expects all selection pressures to point the same way picks this. Crenicichla had been favouring fewer, smaller spots; the spots increased only once that opposing pressure was largely removed.
A student who thinks each bout of selection needs a fresh mutation picks this. The source population already varied in spot number and size; only allele frequencies changed.

In the original stream, natural selection by Crenicichla favoured dull, small-spotted males while females favoured bright ones. Moving the fish to a stream with only a weak predator greatly reduced one of the two opposing pressures, so alleles for more and larger spots increased in frequency.
A student who thinks acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Spot pattern is genetically determined; the change over generations was a change in allele frequencies, not in individual fish.

mcqs.q: In greenhouse ponds, Endler kept guppy populations on coarse or fine gravel with either the dangerous predator Crenicichla, the weak predator Rivulus, or no predator. At the start, males had a mean of about 10 coloured spots each. After about ten generations the mean was about 13 spots per male in ponds with no predator and in ponds with Rivulus, but about 9.5 spots per male in ponds with Crenicichla. In Crenicichla ponds the spots were also close in size to the gravel particles, whereas in no-predator ponds they were not. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The alleles for small spots arose by mutation in each pond only after the predators were added to it
Because spot size came to match gravel size, the females must also have preferred males whose spots matched the gravel
Males in the Crenicichla ponds grew smaller, gravel-matched spots during their lives and passed them on to their sons
The direction of selection on spot pattern depended on the predation pressure that was applied
mcqs.specStatementText: Endler's guppies: selection pressures under experimental control
mcqs.explain: The experiment controlled the selection pressures. Strong predation by Crenicichla selected for camouflage (fewer, gravel-matched spots) and spot number fell; with no predator, or only the weak predator Rivulus, sexual selection alone acted and spot number rose. The same starting population evolved in opposite directions.
rationales: A student who thinks selection needs a new mutation each time picks this. Ten generations is far too short for new alleles to appear and spread in every pond; existing variation was selected.

A student who assumes predators and females favour the same trait picks this. Matching the gravel was favoured only where predators were present; without predators, spot size did not match the gravel, so female preference cannot have been for gravel-matched spots.

A student who thinks acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Spot pattern is genetically determined; the change over ten generations was a change in allele frequencies caused by differential survival and mating, not a change within individual fish.

The experiment controlled the selection pressures. Strong predation by Crenicichla selected for camouflage (fewer, gravel-matched spots) and spot number fell; with no predator, or only the weak predator Rivulus, sexual selection alone acted and spot number rose. The same starting population evolved in opposite directions.

mcqs.q: A pond contains a population of 500 water snails. Which statement best describes the gene pool of this population?
options: All the genes, and all the different alleles of those genes, carried by the 500 snails in the pond
The complete set of genes in one water snail, which is the same in every member of the species
The set of allele frequencies shared by every population of this snail species wherever it lives
Only the alleles natural selection has favoured, because alleles reducing fitness are removed
mcqs.explain: A gene pool consists of all the genes and their different alleles present in a population. It belongs to the interbreeding group, here the 500 snails, and natural selection changes the frequencies of alleles within it.
rationales: A gene pool consists of all the genes and their different alleles present in a population. It belongs to the interbreeding group, here the 500 snails, and natural selection changes the frequencies of alleles within it.

A student who confuses gene pool with genome picks this. A genome is the genetic material of one individual; the gene pool is the total of all alleles in the whole population, and individuals differ in which alleles they carry.

A student who expects every population of a species to have the same allele frequencies picks this. Each separate population has its own gene pool, and populations of one species in different ponds can have different allele frequencies.
A student who thinks selection eliminates unfavourable alleles at once picks this. The gene pool includes every allele present, including rare harmful recessive alleles hidden in heterozygotes.

mcqs.q: A student searches an allele frequency database for the ABO blood group allele Iᴮ. The database gives a frequency of about 0.25 for a population in Central Asia and about 0.01 for an Indigenous population in South America. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The two populations cannot belong to the same species, because members of one species share the same allele frequencies
The two populations have separate gene pools that have diverged in allele frequency while remaining one species
About 25% of the people in the Central Asian population have blood group B, since the allele frequency is 0.25
The Iᴮ allele will spread through the South American population because it is dominant to the allele i
mcqs.specStatementText: Isolated populations drift apart in allele frequency
mcqs.explain: Geographically isolated populations of the same species can have different allele frequencies, because natural selection, genetic drift and founder effects act separately on each gene pool. Both populations are Homo sapiens; only the frequency of Iᴮ differs.
rationales: A student who expects a species to be genetically uniform picks this. Populations of one species commonly differ in allele frequencies; the human ABO alleles are a well-documented example.

Geographically isolated populations of the same species can have different allele frequencies, because natural selection, genetic drift and founder effects act separately on each gene pool. Both populations are Homo sapiens; only the frequency of Iᴮ differs.

A student who takes the allele frequency to be the proportion of people carrying Iᴮ picks this: 25% carry it and, since Iᴮ is dominant to i, they reason that 25% show group B. A frequency of 0.25 is the fraction of allele copies that are Iᴮ; the proportion of people with group B depends on the genotype frequencies and cannot be read off directly.

A student who thinks dominant alleles spread because they are dominant picks this. Dominance affects the phenotype of heterozygotes, not allele frequency; under Hardy–Weinberg conditions a rare dominant allele stays rare.

mcqs.q: A recessive allele causes a condition that is lethal before reproductive age in homozygotes. Heterozygotes are unaffected. Which statement describes how natural selection changes the frequency of this allele in the gene pool?
options: It is removed from the gene pool within a generation, because every individual carrying it dies
It falls because the allele mutates back into the normal allele in individuals who need it in order to survive
It falls slowly over many generations, because the allele is hidden from selection in heterozygotes
It falls rapidly because the dominant normal allele out-competes the recessive allele in each generation
mcqs.specStatementText: Neo-Darwinism: selection as changing allele frequencies
mcqs.explain: Natural selection acts on heritable differences between individuals, that is on phenotypes. Only homozygotes are selected against, and as the allele becomes rarer a smaller fraction of its copies are in homozygotes, so its frequency declines more and more slowly.
rationales: A student who pictures selection acting directly on alleles picks this. Heterozygotes carry the allele but are unaffected, so they survive and pass it on.
A student who thinks mutation is directed by need picks this. Mutation is random and rare; the change in frequency is due to differential survival of genotypes, not to back-mutation.

Natural selection acts on heritable differences between individuals, that is on phenotypes. Only homozygotes are selected against, and as the allele becomes rarer a smaller fraction of its copies are in homozygotes, so its frequency declines more and more slowly.

A student who thinks dominance itself drives frequency change picks this. Dominance describes the heterozygote phenotype; here it is the reason the recessive allele is protected from selection, not removed.

mcqs.q: What is meant by neo-Darwinism?
options: A theory that replaced natural selection after it was shown to be wrong
Darwin's original proposal that species are not fixed but change over time
The idea that characteristics acquired in life can be passed on to the offspring
The integration of genetics with Darwin's theory of natural selection
mcqs.specStatementText: Neo-Darwinism: selection as changing allele frequencies
mcqs.explain: Darwin developed natural selection without knowledge of genes. Biologists subsequently combined Mendelian inheritance, mutation and allele frequencies with natural selection; this integrated theory is known as neo-Darwinism.
rationales: A student who reads 'neo' as a replacement picks this. Neo-Darwinism keeps natural selection as the mechanism and adds the genetic basis of variation and inheritance.

A student who thinks Darwin's contribution was the idea of evolution itself picks this. Evolution was already widely accepted in Darwin's time; neo-Darwinism refers to the later synthesis with genetics.

A student who believes acquired characteristics are inherited assumes the up-to-date theory must include that idea. Inheritance of acquired characteristics is Lamarckism, which Darwin's theory replaced; neo-Darwinism explains inheritance through alleles.

Darwin developed natural selection without knowledge of genes. Biologists subsequently combined Mendelian inheritance, mutation and allele frequencies with natural selection; this integrated theory is known as neo-Darwinism.

mcqs.q: In a study of human births in the mid-twentieth century, babies of intermediate birth mass had the highest survival, while both very light and very heavy babies had higher mortality. Which type of selection does this show, and why?
options: Stabilizing selection, because individuals with intermediate values of the trait are favoured over both extremes
Disruptive selection, because the extremes of the range are disrupted by being selected against
Directional selection, because whenever one phenotype is favoured over others the selection is directional
No selection, because the mean birth mass of the population does not change from generation to generation
mcqs.explain: Selection against both extremes with the intermediate phenotype favoured is stabilizing selection. The mean birth mass is unchanged but variation is reduced, and alleles contributing to extreme birth mass fall in frequency.
rationales: Selection against both extremes with the intermediate phenotype favoured is stabilizing selection. The mean birth mass is unchanged but variation is reduced, and alleles contributing to extreme birth mass fall in frequency.
A student who applies the everyday meaning of 'disruptive' picks this. Disruptive selection favours both extremes over the intermediate, the opposite of this pattern.
A student who uses directional as the default label picks this. Directional selection favours one extreme and shifts the mean; favouring the intermediate is stabilizing selection.
A student who judges selection by the mean alone picks this. Differential survival among phenotypes is selection even when the mean is constant; the variance and the allele frequencies change.

mcqs.q: Which statement about directional, disruptive and stabilizing selection is correct?
options: Stabilizing selection leaves allele frequencies unchanged, since the mean phenotype does not shift
All three types of selection result in a change in the allele frequencies of the gene pool
Disruptive selection is selection that follows a sudden disruption of the environment
Only directional selection results in some phenotypes leaving more offspring than others
mcqs.explain: In each type some phenotypes leave more offspring than others, so the alleles associated with the favoured phenotypes increase in frequency. This is true of stabilizing selection as well, where alleles for the extremes are removed.
rationales: A student who reads a constant mean as a constant gene pool picks this. Stabilizing selection removes alleles for extreme phenotypes, which is a change in allele frequency.

In each type some phenotypes leave more offspring than others, so the alleles associated with the favoured phenotypes increase in frequency. This is true of stabilizing selection as well, where alleles for the extremes are removed.
A student who applies the everyday meaning of 'disruptive' picks this. Disruptive selection is defined by favouring both extremes; a sudden change favouring one extreme causes directional selection.
A student who treats directional selection as the only real kind picks this. All three types involve differential reproductive success; they differ in which part of the range is favoured.

mcqs.q: In a large population, 16% of individuals show the phenotype of the homozygous recessive genotype for a gene with two alleles. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype?
mcqs.explain: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. The homozygous dominant frequency is p² = 0.6² = 0.36. (Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.48, and 0.36 + 0.48 + 0.16 = 1.)
rationales: A student who takes p² to be the frequency of the dominant phenotype picks 1 − 0.16 = 0.84. That is p² + 2pq, which includes the 0.48 of heterozygotes; the homozygous dominant genotype alone is p² = 0.36.
A student who sets q equal to the recessive phenotype frequency (q = 0.16, p = 0.84) gets p² = 0.7056. The recessive phenotype frequency is q², so q = √0.16 = 0.4.
q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. The homozygous dominant frequency is p² = 0.6² = 0.36. (Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.48, and 0.36 + 0.48 + 0.16 = 1.)

A student who does not distinguish allele frequency from genotype frequency stops at p = 0.6. That is the frequency of the dominant allele; the frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype is p² = 0.36.

mcqs.q: A recessive condition affects 1 in 100 individuals in a large population that is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What proportion of the population are heterozygous carriers of the allele?
mcqs.explain: q² = 0.01, so q = 0.1 and p = 0.9. The heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18, so 18% of the population are carriers, eighteen times the number actually affected.
rationales: A student who calculates the heterozygote frequency as p × q gets 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09. The heterozygote can be formed in two ways, so the term is 2pq = 0.18.
A student who takes q = 0.01 (the phenotype frequency) and p = 0.99 gets 2pq = 0.0198. The phenotype frequency is q², so q = √0.01 = 0.1.
A student who treats the allele frequency as the proportion of carriers stops at q = 0.1. The allele frequency is 0.1, but the proportion of individuals heterozygous for it is 2pq = 0.18.
q² = 0.01, so q = 0.1 and p = 0.9. The heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18, so 18% of the population are carriers, eighteen times the number actually affected.

mcqs.q: In a population of 1000 plants, the frequencies of alleles R and r are 0.6 and 0.4. The Hardy–Weinberg equation predicts 360 RR, 480 Rr and 160 rr plants. A survey finds 460 RR, 280 Rr and 260 rr. What can be concluded?
options: At least one Hardy–Weinberg condition is not being met, such as random mating or equal survival of the genotypes
The shortage of heterozygous plants proves that natural selection is acting against the Rr genotype
The population is in genetic equilibrium, because the two allele frequencies still add up to exactly 1
The dominant allele R is replacing r, because dominant alleles increase in frequency over the generations
mcqs.specStatementText: When Hardy–Weinberg holds, and what a misfit means
mcqs.explain: The allele frequencies calculated from the survey are still 0.6 and 0.4 (1200 R copies out of 2000), but the genotype frequencies do not fit p², 2pq, q²: there are too few heterozygotes. This indicates that a condition is broken, for example non-random mating (like mating with like) or differing survival, and further evidence is needed to decide which.
rationales: The allele frequencies calculated from the survey are still 0.6 and 0.4 (1200 R copies out of 2000), but the genotype frequencies do not fit p², 2pq, q²: there are too few heterozygotes. This indicates that a condition is broken, for example non-random mating (like mating with like) or differing survival, and further evidence is needed to decide which.

A student who reaches for natural selection as the only explanation picks this. A deficit of heterozygotes is also produced by non-random mating; the data cannot distinguish between the possible broken conditions.

A student who treats p + q = 1 as a test of equilibrium picks this. p + q = 1 is true of any two-allele population by definition; equilibrium is tested by whether the genotype frequencies fit p² + 2pq + q².

A student who thinks dominance drives allele frequency picks this. The frequency of R in the survey is still 0.6; it is the genotype frequencies, not the allele frequencies, that depart from the prediction.

mcqs.q: After an antibiotic is used repeatedly in a hospital, the proportion of bacteria resistant to it rises sharply. Which statement correctly classifies this change?
options: Artificial selection, because the change in the bacterial population was caused by a human action
Natural selection, because the antibiotic acted as a selection pressure and nobody chose which bacteria bred
Natural selection, because the bacteria mutated to become resistant in response to their exposure to the antibiotic
Artificial selection, because the resistance allele was produced by the human use of the antibiotic
mcqs.explain: Artificial selection requires deliberate human choice of traits for breeding. Here the increase in resistance is an unintended consequence of a human action: the antibiotic killed susceptible bacteria and the resistant ones survived and reproduced, which is natural selection.
rationales: A student who defines artificial selection as 'caused by humans' picks this. The guide is explicit that unintended consequences of human actions, such as antibiotic resistance, are due to natural selection.

Artificial selection requires deliberate human choice of traits for breeding. Here the increase in resistance is an unintended consequence of a human action: the antibiotic killed susceptible bacteria and the resistant ones survived and reproduced, which is natural selection.
A student who thinks mutations are directed by need picks this. Resistance alleles arose by random mutation before exposure; the antibiotic selected the bacteria that already carried them.
A student who thinks humans create the alleles they select picks this. Neither natural nor artificial selection creates alleles; both change the frequencies of alleles that arose by mutation.

mcqs.q: How is artificial selection carried out in a crop plant such as wheat?
options: By creating brand-new alleles for the desired traits and inserting them into the plants
By exposing the crop to a pesticide so that only the pesticide-resistant plants evolve
By choosing the plants with the most desirable traits and breeding only from them
By growing the plants in rich soil so that the better growth passes to seeds
mcqs.explain: Artificial selection is the deliberate choice of traits: in crop plants and domesticated animals, humans select the individuals with desirable traits, such as high yield, to breed from, so the alleles for those traits increase in frequency over generations.
rationales: A student who confuses breeding with genetic modification picks this. Artificial selection uses variation already present; breeders choose which plants reproduce and do not make new alleles.
A student who classes every human-caused change as artificial selection picks this. Resistance evolving in response to a chemical is an unintended consequence, due to natural selection.

Artificial selection is the deliberate choice of traits: in crop plants and domesticated animals, humans select the individuals with desirable traits, such as high yield, to breed from, so the alleles for those traits increase in frequency over generations.
A student who thinks acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Growth gained from good soil is not encoded in the plants' genes and is not passed on; only inherited traits can be selected.

specStatements.text: Natural selection: the mechanism, and the paradigm shift it caused
Too many offspring, too few resources
Adaptation, fitness and competition within a species
Endler's guppies: selection pressures under experimental control
Isolated populations drift apart in allele frequency
Neo-Darwinism: selection as changing allele frequencies
When Hardy–Weinberg holds, and what a misfit means

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Competition is treated as competition between individuals of the same species, and fitness is treated as the survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype. Interspecific competition, niche theory and mathematical measures of relative fitness (selection coefficients) are not included.

Endler's field and greenhouse experiments are used only as data to interpret, described in the stems in words and, for the greenhouse ponds, approximate mean spot numbers. Items do not ask for dates, sample sizes, the statistical tests Endler used, or the taxonomy of the predators beyond naming them.

All Hardy–Weinberg items use exactly two alleles at one locus, denoted p and q. No item involves three or more alleles, sex-linked loci, or chi-squared testing of observed against expected genotype counts.
